title: Observability fire-drill: request reconstruction & error forensics - SummitWell
summary: Redwood demo of Console request reconstruction and error-forensics. Focus on replaying a problematic request path, understanding KV cache fallbacks, model variant failover, and audit/log retention. Customer interested in on-prem vs hosted tradeoffs, SOC2/KMS controls, and a pilot next quarter.
action_items: Alex Rivera - Share dedicated pricing sheet and pilot proposal - due 2026-11-18
Priya Anand - Upload sample anonymized request logs and retention policy - due 2026-11-16
Maya Chen - Prepare small repro runbook and benchmark steps for pilot - due 2026-11-19
next_steps: Alex to send SOC2 artifact pack + network architecture notes
Schedule 1-hour pilot kickoff with SummitWell SREs (Proposed: Nov 24)
Run a 2-hour replay of a high-latency request during pilot week with logs shared
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Patel (SRE, SummitWell), Priya Anand (Platform Eng, SummitWell), Evan Lee (Dir MLOps, SummitWell)

Summary: quick demo of Redwood Console's request reconstruction and error-forensics features. Walked through a synthetic 'fire-drill' where a multi-turn inference request failed with a fallback to smaller model, KV cache miss, and a retry loop. Discussed security, data residency, and pilot criteria.

[00:00] Alex Rivera: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex with redwood inference, maya's on the call to drive the demo. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Jordan Patel: hey alex, thanks, good, we got a little group here, priy a and evan, nice to meet you.
[00:12] Priya Anand: hi all, thanks for doing the drill. we wanted to see the exact steps if we had an incident like last week, you know, where a batch of requests spiked latency.
[00:20] Alex Rivera: yeah absolutely, that's the idea of today's session — observational fire-drill, reconstructing the request, seeing the trace, KV cash — sorry, KV cache — and then the fallback behavior. maya, take it away?
[00:30] Maya Chen: sure, i'll share my screen, okay can you see my console?
[00:36] Jordan Patel: yep, it's coming up.
[00:38] Maya Chen: great. quick housekeeping: our demo environment is a sandbox with a synthetic model that mirrors your latency patterns, so numbers are illustrative. i will trigger a recorded request and show the reconstruction.
[00:48] [02:10] Maya Chen: here in the request-inspector we have the original request payload, you can see headers, time stamps, tokenization, and the execution path. notice the first call went to model v1-large, we then show a 2nd call that attempted to use the kv cache for a prefix hit but it missed — marked as "KV miss" in the console.
[02:35] Jordan Patel: said kv miss, what do you show for cache key? sometimes our keys include user id + conversation id which we redacted?
[02:44] Maya Chen: yep, we mask PII by default in the hosted demo; keys are hashed. it shows the cache key fingerprint and hit/miss rate. there's a small transcription hiccup — sometimes it shows "KV cash" in the log, ignore that, its the speech to text artifact.
[03:05] [05:01] Maya Chen: next you can see an automated timeline: token generation time per chunk, and then a fallback rule triggered — because v1-large exceeded the 2000ms soft SLO, the routing policy fell back to v1-medium after three retries. that fallback event is annotated in the trace and tied to the original request ID.
[05:25] Evan Lee: so the fallbacks are policy-driven; can we tie that to tenancy? we want fallbacks to happen in dedicated capacity only if region X is overloaded, otherwise use hosted cheaper model.
[05:40] Maya Chen: yes the routing policies can be hierarchical — region, capacity type, and customer tier are all selectors. you can compose them so a specific route will prefer dedicated GPU pool first then hosted as fallback or vice versa.
[05:55] [07:20] Jordan Patel: can you replay the exact timeline from the moment the request entered our system to the model selection? that's the part we struggled to reconstruct last week.
[07:30] Maya Chen: absolutely — i'll hit 'reconstruct' — this will stitch together request logs, per-token traces, and infra metrics. it brings up a time-aligned view: load balancer latencies, gateway retries, and the model serving timeline.
[07:48] [09:05] Maya Chen: see at 00:00:01 the gateway forwarded with a 120ms overhead, at 00:00:02 model started, then at 00:00:02.4 we hit a KV miss and started a model cold-start path for the quantized kernel. that cold-start added ~700ms. the console annotates cold-starts, kernel compilation, and if the runtime selected a fallback kernel for quantized op.
[09:30] Priya Anand: okay that kernel compilation note — is that from our side or the runtime? we have our own container start times for private deployments.
[09:40] Maya Chen: it's runtime-level instrumentation. in Private you can surface the same traces into your own observability but the annotations will still show kernel compile and NVTX-like markers. for dedicated and private you can toggle more verbose runtime tracing to see syscalls and GPU utilization.
[09:58] [11:12] Jordan Patel: how granular are the logs we get? retention is a big ask for us — we need 90 days of audit-level request metadata but only 7 days of full token payloads.
[11:24] Alex Rivera: good question, we support tiered retention: audit metadata (request id, timestamps, routing decision) can be kept 90+ days, whereas payloads and tokens can be configured to shorter retention or redacted at ingest based on your policy. Priya, we can share our default retention matrix in the security pack.
[11:48] [13:00] Evan Lee: and encryption at rest? we use an HSM for key management across our infra.
[13:07] Maya Chen: yes KMS integrations supported — AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and we have HSM options for private deployments. keys never leave your account for private; for hosted we can use customer-managed keys within supported clouds.
[13:22] Jordan Patel: we also need SAML SSO / SCIM for team provisioning and RBAC for routes.
[13:29] Alex Rivera: yep supported, we can add that to the pilot checklist.
[13:35] [15:15] Maya Chen: going back to the replay — i clicked 'playback' and you can watch the request step-by-step: the console replays each event, you can jump to the falldown for KV miss, inspect tensor shapes, and also view the model logits at that moment if you have access. in practice we wire the playback to a dumper that can be run in a separate sandbox to safely reproduce.
[15:40] Priya Anand: is there any risk of re-playing sensitive PII into an external model in hosted mode? our compliance team freaks out about re-injecting data.
[15:55] Maya Chen: good catch. playback in hosted mode uses redacted payloads by default; we also support synthetic replay where we replace user tokens with placeholders. for private or dedicated, replay runs inside your VPC so no data leaves your network.
[16:10] [17:45] Jordan Patel: what about alerting and automated runbooks? can we attach an automation to the trace that says, on fallback to smaller model, trigger a rollout rollback?
[17:56] Maya Chen: yes you can wire alerts — console supports webhook integrations to your pager, and you can attach runbook links or automated remediation that triggers a canary rollback or scales dedicated pools. we demonstrated a canary rollback earlier in a separate demo.
[18:15] Evan Lee: does the console preserve exact timing so that our downstream correlators can stitch the request with our internal logs? we rely on microsecond sync.
[18:25] Maya Chen: timestamps are ns-precision where available; we provide correlator IDs (a request trace ID) you can join on. we also ingest your upstream LB traces if you push them to our collector.
[18:35] [19:50] Priya Anand: i'd like to test a scenario where a model variant returns significantly different text causing a downstream confidence drop. can the console compare outputs across variants?
[19:58] Maya Chen: yes there's a response-diff view — side-by-side of tokens, probabilities (approx), and similarity metrics. you can attach evaluation prompt sets to watch for regressions.
[20:20] [22:05] Jordan Patel: earlier you mentioned 'automated timeline' and kernel selection. we had cases where quantization introduced quality drift — can we force not to use quantized kernels for some routes?
[22:18] Maya Chen: absolutely — you can pin a model variant or a kernel profile per route. policies can say: prefer quantized for cost-efficiency but opt-out for safety-critical routes.
[22:35] [24:00] Maya Chen: i'm going to switch to the error analysis tab — this pulls all errors tied to request IDs. notice grouping by error fingerprint; similar stacktraces are clustered and sample requests are surfaced. from there you can open the corresponding trace playback.
[24:20] Jordan Patel: do we get stack traces from the runtime? some of our stack frames are internal and we don't want them leaked.
[24:30] Maya Chen: for hosted, stack frames are redacted unless you enable deeper debug sharing. for private, you control what gets sent to the console. we also provide redaction templates.
[24:46] [26:10] Evan Lee: in terms of pilot, what would success look like for us? our bar is: p95 generation latency < 300ms for standard prompts, fallback incidence < 0.5% during peak, and integrated audit logs for compliance.
[26:24] Alex Rivera: perfect — we can map those to SLOs in the pilot. we propose a 4-week pilot: week 0 onboarding and auth, week 1 baseline replay of last month logs, week 2 live replay & canary, week 3 measurement and handoff.
[26:45] [28:05] Priya Anand: timeline wise we want a pilot start before December due to regulatory review in Jan. can you make onboarding earlier?
[28:12] Alex Rivera: yes we'll aim to start Nov 24 if we close the pilot paperwork this week.
[28:20] [30:00] Maya Chen: one more feature — request lineage. you can trace a user request across multi-step pipelines if you're doing tool-calling or function invocations. it stitches the external API calls and shows downstream latencies.
[30:18] Jordan Patel: hmm we do a lot of tool-calling into internal clinical inference, that would help.
[30:25] Maya Chen: you can register those outbound hooks in the console and those events show up in the same trace.
[30:35] [31:45] Priya Anand: said earlier about private deployment options — cost delta between hosted and private dedicated — can you ballpark?
[31:55] Alex Rivera: ballpark depends on committed capacity; hosted is pay-as-you-go (per-token and per-embed), dedicated is reserved pool pricing with lower per-token unit cost but monthly commit. private adds platform license. i'll send a detailed sheet.
[32:15] Evan Lee: do you support air-gapped on-prem? our security reqs might need it.
[32:21] Maya Chen: yes we have an on-prem package; the control plane can be customer-managed and offline. some advanced observability features require connectors but we can provide offline-compatible artifacts.
[32:35] [34:00] Jordan Patel: ok, can you show how we would triage the exact incident we had last week? i uploaded a sample log earlier to the shared drive.
[34:12] Maya Chen: let me pull that in... okay i've loaded the anonymized log, hitting 'reconstruct incident'...
[34:28] [36:05] Maya Chen: here the console automatically maps your load balancer entry ID to a request trace and pulls in the next hops. you can see a retry storm between 14:23:10 and 14:23:22 which correlates to our autoscaler oscillation. the request trace shows 18 retries from the gateway due to transient model OOM and then a fallback that caused response mismatch.
[36:40] Priya Anand: oh interesting the autoscaler oscillation — we saw similar signs, but couldn't get the internal model OOM footprint. do you record GPU OOM events in the trace?
[36:50] Maya Chen: yes OOMs are annotated; you can group by OOM cause and get the container logs. in private you get full logs, in hosted we provide summarized events and can run isolated repros.
[37:05] [38:20] Evan Lee: what's the overhead of enabling verbose tracing? we worry about performance impact during production.
[38:28] Maya Chen: verbose traces add minimal CPU overhead but a small metadata ingestion cost; we've measured <2% end-to-end overhead when tracing is on. for high-throughput routes you can sample traces.
[38:45] [40:00] Jordan Patel: how does the eve fallback interact with model caching? we have a pattern where the KV cache warms slowly and causes an initial hit spike.
[40:12] Maya Chen: rewarming is a thing — console can surface warm/cold windows and we offer a warmup policy to pre-warm frequently used prefixes during traffic spikes. also cache eviction policies are configurable.
[40:30] Priya Anand: would we be able to hook our own cache metrics into the console?
[40:36] Maya Chen: yes you can push metrics via prometheus or our agent, and they stitch into the timeline.
[40:45] [42:10] Alex Rivera: quick check — any blockers from security side that would prevent a pilot?
[42:18] Priya Anand: main blockers are KMS/HSM proof, audit retention mapping, and confirmation we can run replay in our VPC.
[42:30] Alex Rivera: we'll include KMS docs and a private replay runbook in the pack.
[42:40] [44:05] Jordan Patel: one more Q — can the console generate a compliance report for an incident that we can hand to auditors?
[44:12] Maya Chen: yes there's an incident export that includes timeline, routing decisions, hashes of payloads, and an audit trail. it redacts as configured and can be signed.
[44:25] [46:00] Evan Lee: overall i'm happy — the ability to run a contained replay inside our network and get timeline-level granularity seems to solve most of our pains.
[46:12] Priya Anand: agreed. next steps from our side: i'll get the sanitized logs up and confirm a list of STAKEHOLDERS for the pilot.
[46:20] Alex Rivera: perfect. i'll follow up with the security pack, pilot proposal, and pricing. maya will own the runbook.
[46:30] [48:00] Maya Chen: before we finish, quick demo note: some product names may be mis-transcribed in the recording, e.g., 'redwood dedicate' vs dedicated, 'KV cash' — so please reference the feature names in the docs i'll send.
[48:15] Jordan Patel: noted, thanks.
[48:20] [50:00] Alex Rivera: i'll recap quickly: 1) send SOC2/KMS and retention matrix, 2) propose pilot start date Nov 24, 3) maya will provide the replay runbook and prepare a short benchmark. any objections?
[50:12] Priya Anand: no objections.
[50:20] Evan Lee: thumbs up.
[50:25] Jordan Patel: thanks everyone.
[50:30] Alex Rivera: thanks all, we'll send notes and next steps.
[50:35] [51:50] Meeting end: 15:52 UTC

Questions captured:
- How are KV cache keys masked during playback?
- What is the overhead of verbose tracing in production?
- Can playback run entirely inside SummitWell VPC?
